The model reuses its middle layers 3 times per token instead of adding more weights. That keeps the checkpoint near 20GB, small enough for a 32GB Mac or 1 NVIDIA DGX Spark. For developers, Inkling 2 Mini is a local option for agentic coding, tool use and document work. It ships under Apache 2.0 on Hugging Face , with hosted inference and fine-tuning on Tinker . TL;DR Size: 26.4B total, 3.4B active (5.4B effective per token with looping), up to 1M-token context. Runs on: Apple silicon with 32GB+ memory, 1 NVIDIA DGX Spark, or GPUs with 32GB+ VRAM. GGUF builds via Unsloth and llama.cpp. Performance: 20.1 on the Artificial Analysis Index, tied with Qwen3.8-27B (self-reported). Best: 79.2% on SWE-bench Verified (bash only). Worst: 15.2% on HLE-Diamond and 50.0% on MultiChallenge. Bottom line: Best: strong agentic coding from a 20GB checkpoint. Worst: weaker knowledge recall and multi-turn instruction following. What is Inkling 2 Mini? Inkling 2 Mini is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts model from Thinking Machines that loops its middle layers. It accepts text and images and returns text only. It follows Inkling 2 Small, a 594B-parameter model released on November 5. How does the looped transformer work? The model stores 24 layers, grouped into 4 blocks of 6. The first and last blocks run once. The 2 middle blocks run 3 times with shared weights. That gives 48 layer applications per token from 24 layers of weights. Each pass after the first receives a “message” from the previous pass. Thinking Machines carries it with Attention Residuals and a learned gate. Feed-forward layers use 128 experts, with 8 routed per token. Looping the middle layers gave a 1.51x to 1.91x compute-equivalent gain. Looping the last layers gave only 1.24x to 1.36x. The middle-loop variant won 27 of 28 evaluations. Looping costs training compute but saves inference. An unlooped baseline used 7.5% less training compute. It needed 140% more inference compute to match the looped model’s loss on 512k-token agentic traces. How was Inkling 2 Mini trained? Training began with 384 experts per layer, with 8 active per token. At midtraining, the team pruned two-thirds of them and kept the 128 most-used experts. A 1T-token distillation run from a larger internal Inkling model then healed the pruned model. Post-training used SFT, then RL over 2.2T tokens and 2,000 steps, plus on-policy distillation. Expert layers are trained and deployed in NVFP4. The last 4 layers use MXFP8. Thinking Machines says this removes quantization conversion loss. A research variant, TML-d24-varloop-research , trains with 1 to 5 passes. How does Inkling 2 Mini perform on benchmarks? All Inkling scores below are self-reported by Thinking Machines. Coding is the strongest area. Inkling 2 Mini scores 79.2% on SWE-bench Verified (bash only) and 77.9% on SWE-bench Pro v2 (Hard). It reaches 48.2% on DeepSWE v1.1, where Qwen’s own card lists Qwen3.8-27B at 42.2%. On Terminal Bench v2.1 it scores 71.6%, behind Qwen3.8-27B at 73.0%. Agentic search also holds up: 79.0% on BrowseComp with compaction and 82.7% on MCP Atlas. For documents and vision, it posts 92.8% on OmniDocBench v1.6 and 74.9% on MMMU Pro. It lists Qwen3.6-35B-A3B at 0.430 and Gemma-4-26B-A4B at 0.159. How does Inkling 2 Mini compare with Qwen and Gemma? The post Best Personal AI Agents in 2026: OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, Gemini Spark and More, Compared on Memory, Security and Cost appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> A personal AI agent runs continuously, keeps memory across sessions, and acts inside your apps. You talk to it in a chat app, by email or by voice. It keeps working after you close the window. The category started small. OpenClaw began in November 2025 as Clawdbot, a weekend project by Peter Steinberger. Twelve months later, Google, OpenAI, Meta and Perplexity all ship their own versions. The products split into 2 camps. Self-hosted agents run on your machine or server and use any model you choose. Managed agents run on a vendor’s cloud VM and come bundled with a subscription. How we ranked them We scored each agent on 3 axes that matter once an agent holds your inbox and credentials. Memory: what persists, where it is stored, and whether you can read, edit or delete it. Security: default permissions, the isolation boundary, approval gates, and the public incident record. Cost: the subscription price, or token spend plus hosting for self-hosted options. Facts come from vendor documentation, launch posts and independent security research. Prices are US list prices as of November 21, 2026. Ranking reflects overall fit for an individual user, not raw capability. Comparison table Rank Agent Maker Runs on Memory Security default Starting cost Best for 1 Hermes Agent Nous Research Your machine or server; Docker, Modal, Daytona backends MEMORY.md, USER.md, SQLite FTS5 session search, self-written skills Manual approvals, denied on timeout; hardline denylist Free (MIT) + model tokens Developers who want an agent that learns 2 OpenClaw OpenClaw Foundation Your machine or server; opt-in sandbox Editable Markdown workspace files; SQLite sessions since 2.0 Full host access unless sandbox is enabled Free (MIT) + tokens; managed hosts ~$12–$49/mo Widest chat-channel reach 3 Gemini Spark Google Dedicated Google Cloud VMs Google account context via connected apps Asks before spending money or sending email $19.99/mo AI Pro (US) Google Workspace users 4 OpenAI dots OpenAI OpenAI cloud computer; optional connected computer Chats, ChatGPT memory and the dot’s own notes Proactive research is read-only; passwords hidden from model Included in eligible ChatGPT Pro and Business Premium plans ChatGPT and Codex power users 5 Meta Muse Meta Muse Secure VM in Meta’s cloud Learns preferences; forgets on request Sentinel agent gates internet access; approvals for email and purchases Free; $20 and $100 tiers Everyday errands on a free tier 6 Perplexity Personal Computer Perplexity Your Mac plus Perplexity cloud Not detailed publicly On-device authorization, 2FA, audit trail Pro or Max subscription Mac users who need local files 7 NanoClaw, IronClaw, ZeroClaw Open-source projects Containers, WebAssembly or a small Rust binary Varies by project Isolation on by default Free + tokens Security-first self-hosters 1. Hermes Agent (Nous Research) What it is : Hermes Agent is an open-source agent from Nous Research. It runs from a terminal UI, a native desktop app , a local web dashboard and messaging gateways. Parallel counts about 25 supported platforms as of October 2026 , including Telegram, Slack, WhatsApp, Signal, Teams and email. Native iMessage arrived in June 2026. Memory : Memory is the main reason to pick Hermes. It keeps persistent MEMORY.md and USER.md files and curates them with periodic nudges. Session history sits in SQLite with FTS5 full-text search and LLM summarization. Pluggable providers include Honcho user modeling plus 8+ community backends. Hermes also writes its own skills. It turns completed complex tasks into reusable skills and refines them over time. Skills follow the agentskills.io standard. The /learn command captures a workflow as a slash command without hand-writing SKILL.md. Security : The docs describe a 7-layer defense-in-depth model . Layers include user allowlists, DM pairing and human approval for destructive commands. Approval mode can be manual, smart (an auxiliary LLM rates risk) or off. The defaults fail closed. An unanswered approval prompt is denied after 300 seconds . Your own deny rules survive even YOLO mode. Nous is explicit about the limits. Its docs say the denylist does not sandbox a hostile or compromised agent. The project’s SECURITY.md names OS-level isolation as the one load-bearing boundary. For broad tool access, use a container backend such as Docker, Modal, Daytona or Vercel Sandbox. Cost : The agent is free. You pay for model tokens from any provider: OpenRouter, OpenAI, Anthropic, or local runtimes like Ollama and vLLM. Nous Portal is optional, with Free, $20, $100 and $200 monthly tiers . Local models cut token spend to zero; see the one-click local model setup . Comments: Hermes is the best open-source pick for most developers. It pairs the deepest memory stack with fail-closed defaults. Setup is still terminal-first, and the local backend offers no protection from a compromised agent. 2. OpenClaw (OpenClaw Foundation) What it is : OpenClaw defined the category. It started in November 2025 as Clawdbot and went viral in January 2026. OpenClaw 2.0 shipped as v2026.8.1 on August 31, 2026 , built by 933 contributors. The latest release we covered is 2026.9.5 , with atomic updates and plugin hot reload. A central Gateway process routes messages, runs cron jobs and hosts a Control UI. OpenClaw reached 26 channels as of v2026.6 , including WhatsApp, Telegram, iMessage, Teams, Matrix and Signal. Supported models include OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, DeepSeek, xAI, Kimi, Ollama and OpenRouter. Memory : OpenClaw stores behavior in human-editable Markdown files. SOUL.md holds the persona, TOOLS.md the tool rules and USER.md what the agent knows about you. Version 2.0 moved session and transcript storage into SQLite for better persistence. This design is transparent. You can open, diff and back up every memory file with ordinary tools. Security : This is OpenClaw’s weak point. The default mode gives full host access , which WIRED called incredibly risky. An opt-in sandbox runs sessions in per-session Docker containers. It defaults to no network egress, a read-only root and all capabilities dropped. The incident record is long. CVE-2026-25253 allowed one-click remote code execution via a WebSocket origin bypass. Visiting a malicious page was enough to steal auth tokens. It was patched quickly. The skills registry was the bigger problem. Koi Security audited 2,857 ClawHub skills and found 341 malicious entries . 335 traced back to one campaign, now tracked as ClawHavoc. Antiy CERT later counted 1,184 malicious skills as the registry grew. OpenClaw responded. It now scans every uploaded skill with VirusTotal and re-scans daily. Version 2.0 added protected credential requests and a team-scoped Secret Store. Treat ClawHub as untrusted code anyway. Cost : OpenClaw is free under MIT. A survey of managed hosts found plans from about $12 to roughly $49 per month . Watch the heartbeat check. With expensive models, it can drive significant token spend. Comments: Pick OpenClaw for channel breadth and the largest ecosystem. Turn on the sandbox, skip unvet

We are looking for one US-based closer for booked calls. The role starts with a paid two-week trial.</p> <p>The work</p> <ul> <li>Our sales are written-first. A prospect replies to our email, receives a free one-page written plan, and picks a call time in writing. You take those booked calls, return calls from prospects who phoned us, and rebook missed calls. No cold dialing and no lists.</li> <li>On each call you qualify, present our written fixed-fee offer (mid four figures to low five figures), confirm who signs, and ask for the decision. We send every agreement and payment link.</li> <li>You send a short written report after each call, the same day.</li> <li>Calls are in US business hours (Eastern Time). You talk to it in a chat app, by email or by voice. It keeps working after you close the window. The category started small. OpenClaw began in November 2025 as Clawdbot, a weekend project by Peter Steinberger. Twelve months later, Google, OpenAI, Meta and Perplexity all ship their own versions. The products split into 2 camps. Self-hosted agents run on your machine or server and use any model you choose. Managed agents run on a vendor’s cloud VM and come bundled with a subscription. How we ranked them We scored each agent on 3 axes that matter once an agent holds your inbox and credentials. Memory: what persists, where it is stored, and whether you can read, edit or delete it. Security: default permissions, the isolation boundary, approval gates, and the public incident record. Cost: the subscription price, or token spend plus hosting for self-hosted options. Facts come from vendor documentation, launch posts and independent security research. Prices are US list prices as of November 21, 2026. Ranking reflects overall fit for an individual user, not raw capability. Hermes Agent (Nous Research) What it is : Hermes Agent is an open-source agent from Nous Research. It runs from a terminal UI, a native desktop app , a local web dashboard and messaging gateways. Parallel counts about 25 supported platforms as of October 2026 , including Telegram, Slack, WhatsApp, Signal, Teams and email. Native iMessage arrived in June 2026. Memory : Memory is the main reason to pick Hermes. It keeps persistent MEMORY.md and USER.md files and curates them with periodic nudges. Session history sits in SQLite with FTS5 full-text search and LLM summarization. Pluggable providers include Honcho user modeling plus 8+ community backends. Hermes also writes its own skills. It turns completed complex tasks into reusable skills and refines them over time. Skills follow the agentskills.io standard. The /learn command captures a workflow as a slash command without hand-writing SKILL.md. Security : The docs describe a 7-layer defense-in-depth model . Layers include user allowlists, DM pairing and human approval for destructive commands. Approval mode can be manual, smart (an auxiliary LLM rates risk) or off. The defaults fail closed. An unanswered approval prompt is denied after 300 seconds . Your own deny rules survive even YOLO mode. Nous is explicit about the limits. Its docs say the denylist does not sandbox a hostile or compromised agent. The project’s SECURITY.md names OS-level isolation as the one load-bearing boundary. For broad tool access, use a container backend such as Docker, Modal, Daytona or Vercel Sandbox. Cost : The agent is free. You pay for model tokens from any provider: OpenRouter, OpenAI, Anthropic, or local runtimes like Ollama and vLLM. Nous Portal is optional, with Free, $20, $100 and $200 monthly tiers . Local models cut token spend to zero; see the one-click local model setup . Comments: Hermes is the best open-source pick for most developers. It pairs the deepest memory stack with fail-closed defaults. Setup is still terminal-first, and the local backend offers no protection from a compromised agent. 2. OpenClaw (OpenClaw Foundation) What it is : OpenClaw defined the category. It started in November 2025 as Clawdbot and went viral in January 2026. OpenClaw 2.0 shipped as v2026.8.1 on August 31, 2026 , built by 933 contributors. The latest release we covered is 2026.9.5 , with atomic updates and plugin hot reload. A central Gateway process routes messages, runs cron jobs and hosts a Control UI. OpenClaw reached 26 channels as of v2026.6 , including WhatsApp, Telegram, iMessage, Teams, Matrix and Signal. Supported models include OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, DeepSeek, xAI, Kimi, Ollama and OpenRouter. Memory : OpenClaw stores behavior in human-editable Markdown files. SOUL.md holds the persona, TOOLS.md the tool rules and USER.md what the agent knows about you. Version 2.0 moved session and transcript storage into SQLite for better persistence. This design is transparent. You can open, diff and back up every memory file with ordinary tools. Security : This is OpenClaw’s weak point. The default mode gives full host access , which WIRED called incredibly risky. An opt-in sandbox runs sessions in per-session Docker containers. It defaults to no network egress, a read-only root and all capabilities dropped. The incident record is long. CVE-2026-25253 allowed one-click remote code execution via a WebSocket origin bypass. Visiting a malicious page was enough to steal auth tokens. It was patched quickly. The skills registry was the bigger problem. Koi Security audited 2,857 ClawHub skills and found 341 malicious entries . 335 traced back to one campaign, now tracked as ClawHavoc. Alpamayo 2 Edge is a 2B-parameter model that plans trajectories and explains them inside the vehicle. It targets NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor , not a datacenter GPU. The goal: reasoning-based planning within onboard compute and latency budgets. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . TL;DR Size: 2B-class. Card breakdown: 2.45B backbone + 0.2B action expert (HF metadata says 3B). Context length: not disclosed (measured prompt: 3,236 tokens). Runs on: NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor with the FP8 + TensorRT Edge-LLM recipe. BF16 PyTorch needs 16 GB+ GPU memory, validated on 1x H100 80GB. Worst: only H100 validated, and real-time Thor speed needs the FP8 recipe. What is Alpamayo 2 Edge? Alpamayo 2 Edge is an open NVIDIA VLA model that turns surround-camera video into a 6.4-second plan. It is the in-car member of the Alpamayo family , next to the 34B cloud model Alpamayo 2 Super . Per the model card , the 2.45B backbone pairs a 1.96B language model with a 0.41B SigLIP2 encoder. A 0.2B diffusion action expert sits on top. The backbone comes from NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Edge and is Nemotron-based. NVIDIA markets the model as 2B, while Hugging Face metadata shows 3B. What goes in and what comes out? For trajectory prediction, the model reads 6 cameras and 22 frames per observation. The 2 front cameras give 5 frames each, the other 4 give 3 each. It also takes a navigation instruction and 20 historical ego poses. Output is 64 waypoints from 0.1 to 6.4 seconds. The action expert predicts acceleration and curvature, then a unicycle model integrates them. The text output is a Chain-of-Causation (CoC) reasoning trace. The model also answers free-form questions about a driving scene. How does adaptive reasoning work? During routine driving, the model emits special <NOMINAL> tokens instead of a full reasoning trace. It writes CoC reasoning only when a scene needs it. Fewer tokens means less compute per planning step. How was Alpamayo 2 Edge trained? NVIDIA team lists these ingredients: Offline distillation from CoC autolabels generated by Alpamayo 2 Super. About 115,000 hours of multi-camera driving video and about 3.7M CoC traces. Closed-loop RL post-training in AlpaGym , learning from its own actions in simulation. Multi-resolution inputs for cheaper encoding of surround views. How fast does it run on DRIVE AGX Thor? Hugging Face weights ship in BF16 and run as a PyTorch model. Real-time use on Thor needs the Alpamayo Developer Hub recipe. On a workstation GPU, the card recommends at least 16 GB of memory. NVIDIA measured 12.06 GiB peak process memory on 1 H100 with 6 trajectory candidates. Other GPU architectures are not yet validated. How does Alpamayo 2 Edge score on benchmarks? NVIDIA compares Edge with Alibaba’s 4B Qwen-Drive-1.0 . The model card adds: AlpaSim: 15.15 ± 0.04 km per at-fault incident over 875 NuRec scenarios, 3 rollouts. Open-loop minADE_6 at 5 s: 0.52 m on 1,392 PhysicalAI-AV samples.
